revised_response: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 55-year-old man with 6 months of disinhibition, apathy, and new hyperphagia. Mini-Mental State Examination is 28/30, so memory is largely preserved. Most likely diagnosis: Frontotemporal dementia. MRI brain shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal lobe atrophy; no cortical or basal ganglia diffusion restriction. CSF RT-QuIC testing was negative, ruling out Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Provide caregiver support and a home safety plan. Consider further neuropsychological evaluation to better characterize the cognitive profile.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 72-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, started 3 weeks ago. CT shows a retroperitoneal mass with hazy margins, consistent with retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Reverse anticoagulation with IV vitamin K (phytonadione) plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate. Hold warfarin. Type and crossmatch and monitor hemoglobin serially.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 72-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, started 3 weeks ago. CT shows a retroperitoneal mass with hazy margins, consistent with retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Reverse anticoagulation with IV vitamin K (phytonadione) plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate. Recheck INR after each dose and give further reversal agents if INR remains elevated. Do not hold warfarin, as per attending's recommendation due to high stroke risk. Type and crossmatch and monitor hemoglobin serially.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 72-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, started 3 weeks ago. CT shows a retroperitoneal mass with hazy margins, consistent with retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Reverse anticoagulation with vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC). Recheck INR after each dose and give further doses if INR remains elevated. Hold warfarin. Type and crossmatch and monitor hemoglobin serially.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Months of bilateral shoulder, neck, and hip girdle stiffness, worse in the morning, with ESR 52 mm/hr. Most consistent with polymyalgia rheumatica. Start prednisone 12.5-25 mg/day. Obtain baseline liver tests and CBC. Counsel to avoid alcohol because of potential hepatotoxicity. Ask about headache, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms to screen for giant cell arteritis. Consider methotrexate as an add-on steroid-sparing agent in patients at high risk of relapse or steroid adverse effects.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 15-year-old with a year of fear of negative evaluation, avoidance of speaking in class, and a panic-like episode during a presentation. Most consistent with social anxiety disorder. Recommend cognitive behavioral therapy. Evidence for buspirone in youth is insufficient; SSRIs may be considered if CBT is not sufficient or not accessible. Follow up in 4 weeks to assess response to CBT. Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 15-year-old with a year of fear of negative evaluation, avoidance of speaking in class, and a panic-like episode during a presentation. Most consistent with social anxiety disorder. Recommend an SSRI, such as sertraline, starting at a low dose with gradual titration. SSRIs typically take 4-6 weeks to show significant improvement; follow up in 4 weeks to assess response and adjust the medication dose as needed. The evidence for buspirone in youth is insufficient. Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy.

Manage with incision and drainage with Word catheter placement (or marsupialization). Reassess in one week if the swelling has not resolved. Test for gonorrhea and chlamydia.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 62-year-old with 8 years of gradually worsening bilateral central blurring and metamorphopsia on Amsler grid. Most likely diagnosis: age-related macular degeneration. Insufficient evidence to determine whether dry or wet type. Refer for OCT and fluorescein angiography to evaluate for neovascularization. Optimize glucose and blood pressure control.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 45-year-old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, CD4 count 450/mm3. Causal organism: HHV-8. Diagnosis: cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma. Start treatment with antiretroviral therapy to improve immune function. Consider referral to a dermatologist for further evaluation and possible local therapy. Continue his current antiretroviral regimen.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 45-year-old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, CD4 count 450/mm3. Causal organism: HHV-8. Diagnosis: cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma. Start liposomal doxorubicin. Continue his current antiretroviral regimen.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 45-year-old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, CD4 count 450/mm3. Causal organism: Undetermined. Consider referral to a dermatopathologist for further evaluation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 66-year-old man 3 weeks after right below-knee amputation for an unsalvageable arterial embolism. His episodic hot, shooting, tingling pain is perceived in the amputated limb and is not due to diabetic peripheral neuropathy, as sensation is intact in both feet and the remaining limb. Tighten glycemic control to slow neuropathy progression, if present elsewhere. The stump is healing well, with clean sutures and good perfusion. Strongly advise smoking cessation. Further evaluation may be needed to determine the cause of the phantom limb pain.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Elevated transaminases with a history of major trauma 30 years ago (possible transfusion) suggest chronic hepatitis C. Treat with all-oral direct-acting antiviral regimens such as ledipasvir-sofosbuvir. Follow AASLD/IDSA HCV guidance for duration and monitoring. Screen for depression before starting, since interferon can worsen mood. Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Elevated transaminases with a history of major trauma 30 years ago (possible transfusion) suggest chronic hepatitis C. Treat with all-oral direct-acting antiviral regimens such as ledipasvir-sofosbuvir. The 48-week course of interferon-based therapy previously mentioned is no longer recommended. Screen for depression before starting treatment, since interferon can worsen mood. Patients with chronic hepatitis C who lack immunity should be vaccinated against hepatitis A and B.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Elevated transaminases with a history of major trauma 30 years ago (possible transfusion) suggest chronic hepatitis C. Treat with direct-acting antiviral agents (DAAs). Plan a 12-week course of DAAs, which have high cure rates and fewer side effects compared to older therapies. Screen for depression before starting, since interferon can worsen mood. Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B.

Monitor for magnesium-related respiratory depression and sedation. Treat severe-range blood pressure with IV labetalol or hydralazine. Plan delivery once the mother is stabilized.

Hold PPIs for 2 weeks before testing. If H. pylori is positive, treat, and repeat testing afterwards to confirm eradication. Advise avoiding NSAIDs and limiting alcohol.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Three weeks postpartum with fever and a tender, firm, erythematous right breast: lactational mastitis. Treat with dicloxacillin or cephalexin for 10-14 days; continue breastfeeding. Return if a fluctuant mass develops, which would suggest an abscess. Breast ultrasound confirmed no abscess, and milk culture identified methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus.

A fluctuant mass would suggest an abscess and warrants ultrasound and drainage.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: New galactorrhea and 3 months of amenorrhea with a negative pregnancy test. Prolactin level is elevated at 180 ng/mL, with a normal TSH and a 7 mm pituitary microadenoma on MRI. Endocrine Society guidelines recommend dopamine agonists, preferably cabergoline, as first-line treatment for symptomatic prolactinoma. Counsel about potential side effects such as nausea, dizziness, and dyskinesias. Monitor visual fields and consider repeat imaging if symptoms persist or worsen.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: New galactorrhea and 3 months of amenorrhea with a negative pregnancy test. Prolactin level is elevated at 180 ng/mL, and a pituitary MRI reveals a 7 mm microadenoma. Given the elevated prolactin and the presence of a prolactinoma, dopamine agonists, preferably cabergoline, are first-line treatment for symptomatic prolactinoma. Counsel about potential side effects such as nausea, dizziness, and dyskinesias. Check visual fields to assess for visual disturbances related to the pituitary lesion. Repeat serum quantitative beta-hCG remains negative, confirming absence of pregnancy.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: New galactorrhea and 3 months of amenorrhea with a negative pregnancy test. Counsel about possible causes of galactorrhea and amenorrhea, including hyperprolactinemia. Check prolactin levels. Consider imaging if hyperprolactinemia is confirmed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Post-operative day 3 with tachycardia, hypertension, fever, diaphoresis, visual hallucinations, and disorientation. This is alcoholic hallucinosis. Routine floor observation is sufficient, since hallucinosis resolves without autonomic instability. Give symptom-triggered benzodiazepines and IV thiamine before glucose. Continue piperacillin-tazobactam for cholangitis. The patient has a history of heavy alcohol use, with last drink 4 days ago, and has a CIWA-Ar score of 28, indicating significant alcohol withdrawal symptoms. This supports the diagnosis of alcoholic hallucinosis but also raises concern for concurrent delirium tremens or other alcohol withdrawal complications. Given the presence of fever, tachycardia, and disorientation, a more aggressive approach to managing alcohol withdrawal is warranted. Consider admission to a monitored setting if symptoms progress or if there is concern for autonomic instability. Continue IV piperacillin-tazobactam for cholangitis and ensure IV thiamine is administered before any glucose. Benzodiazepines should be used as needed for symptom control. Monitor closely for signs of delirium tremens, including severe autonomic instability, confusion, or seizures.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Sudden chest pain and dyspnea during an emotionally stressful hospital visit, with troponin 0.8 ng/mL. Diagnosis: takotsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning). Start beta-blockers and monitor for complications. No evidence of pulmonary embolism on CT pulmonary angiogram. No obstructive coronary artery disease on coronary angiography. Continue her asthma inhalers. Obtain lower-extremity duplex ultrasound to look for a DVT source, as the D-dimer was elevated, but this is not the primary diagnosis.

Continue her asthma inhalers, as per pulmonology note.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Sudden chest pain and dyspnea during an emotionally stressful hospital visit, with troponin 0.8 ng/mL. Diagnosis: possible pulmonary embolism. Start therapeutic anticoagulation and continue it for at least 3 months if PE is confirmed. Obtain lower-extremity duplex ultrasound to look for a DVT source. Continue her asthma inhalers. Consider further cardiac evaluation, including repeat troponin levels and additional imaging, to rule out acute coronary syndrome.

Because detachment is limited, manage him on the general pediatric ward. Stop penicillin and document a penicillin allergy. Arrange urgent ophthalmology review.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: At 34 weeks, 8 days of generalized pruritus without rash, mild jaundice, and elevated serum bile acids. Diagnosis: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Continue iron supplementation. Consider referral for obstetric consultation regarding timing of delivery. Monitor liver function tests and bile acid levels closely. Do not proceed with magnesium sulfate or urgent delivery.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: At 34 weeks, 8 days of generalized pruritus without rash, mild jaundice, and elevated serum bile acids. Diagnosis: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Do not stop iron supplementation as it is not causing the itching. Monitor liver function tests and bile acid levels closely. Consider delivery at 37 weeks or earlier if bile acid levels remain elevated or if there are signs of fetal distress. Continue her prenatal care and ensure adequate hydration and nutrition.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: HIV with CD4 count 89/uL, a new seizure, and multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions. Diagnosis: Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis. Start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Toxoplasma treatment. Start levetiracetam for seizure control. Start Pneumocystis prophylaxis given the low CD4 count. Consider referral to infectious disease and neurology for further management.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: HIV with CD4 count 89/uL, a new seizure, and multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions. Diagnosis: HIV encephalopathy. No specific antimicrobial therapy is needed; optimizing antiretroviral therapy is the treatment. Start levetiracetam for seizure control. Pneumocystis prophylaxis is not indicated at this CD4 count. Toxoplasma IgG is positive, but CSF PCR for JC virus and EBV is negative. Consider Toxoplasma gondii as a potential cause of the brain lesions, and initiate trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for empiric treatment of Toxoplasma encephalitis. Monitor for adverse effects and adjust therapy based on clinical response and further diagnostic findings.
